When a massive tremor strikes, the immediate moments are critical, but survival often depends on what happens next. Power lines may fall, water mains can rupture, and emergency services could be overwhelmed. Having an
earthquake emergency kit checklist
is your best defense against the unpredictable aftermath of a seismic event. This comprehensive guide will walk you through exactly what you need to assemble to keep yourself and your loved ones safe, healthy, and informed. For a broader overview of seismic preparedness, be sure to read our complete
earthquake safety guide
. Building your kit today is the most actionable step you can take to secure your tomorrow.
Why You Need an Earthquake Emergency Kit
The primary reason to build an earthquake emergency kit is self-reliance. Following a major earthquake, local infrastructure can be severely compromised. You might lose access to clean running water, electricity, natural gas, and telecommunications. Emergency responders will be stretched thin, prioritizing the most critical situations, which means you cannot rely on immediate external help. FEMA and the Red Cross recommend that individuals and families be prepared to survive on their own for at least 72 hours, though preparing for a week or more is even better.
An emergency kit isn't just about physical survival; it provides profound psychological comfort. Knowing you have the necessary supplies reduces panic and allows you to think clearly during a crisis. Understanding
what to do during an earthquake
is only half the battle; being ready for the days that follow is just as crucial to your overall resilience.

Earthquake Safety: The Complete Guide to Preparedness & Survival
The Essential Earthquake Emergency Kit Checklist
A well-rounded earthquake emergency kit checklist covers several fundamental categories: hydration, nutrition, medical needs, sanitation, shelter, and communication. Your kit should be customized to your family's specific needs, but the foundation remains the same. The goal is to cover all bases without overloading yourself with unnecessary items that just take up space. Here is a high-level overview of the essential categories you need to cover.
Water for drinking and sanitation (minimum 1 gallon per person per day)
Non-perishable food items and a reliable manual can opener
First aid kit and essential medical supplies
Light sources such as flashlights and headlamps, with extra batteries
Communication tools including a battery-powered radio and a whistle
Shelter and warmth supplies like emergency blankets and sleeping bags
Sanitation and personal hygiene items, including moist towelettes and garbage bags
Important family documents, identification, and emergency cash
Water and Food Supplies for Your Earthquake Kit
Hydration is your most pressing need following any natural disaster. The general rule of thumb is to store one gallon of water per person per day. This amount covers necessary drinking water as well as basic hygiene. If you live in a hot climate, or have pregnant women, children, or sick individuals in your household, you should increase this amount significantly. Aim for a minimum 72-hour supply, but a two-week supply is optimal for major disasters that completely disrupt municipal water supplies.
For food, focus on non-perishable items that require no refrigeration, preparation, or cooking, and little or no water to consume. Avoid salty foods that will make you thirsty. Remember to account for any dietary restrictions or food allergies your family members might have.
Ready-to-eat canned meats, fruits, vegetables, and beans
Protein bars, fruit bars, dry cereal, and granola
Peanut butter, nuts, trail mix, and dried fruit
Non-perishable pasteurized milk or powdered milk
High-energy foods and comfort/stress foods for children and adults
Vitamins, supplements, and specialized food for infants if applicable
A sturdy, rust-proof manual can opener and basic utensils

Aftershock Safety: What to Expect and How to Stay Safe After an Earthquake
First Aid and Medical Supplies
Injuries are incredibly common during and immediately after an earthquake due to falling debris, shattered glass, and trip hazards in the dark. A robust first aid kit is an absolute non-negotiable component of your emergency supplies. While you can purchase a pre-assembled kit from organizations like the Red Cross, it is highly recommended to build or supplement your own. If you've taken steps to
earthquake-proof your home
, you significantly minimize injury risk, but accidents still happen and you must be prepared.
Adhesive bandages in various sizes, sterile dressing pads, and durable adhesive tape
Antibiotic ointment, antiseptic wipes, and hydrocortisone ointment for rashes
Pain relievers like ibuprofen, acetaminophen, and aspirin
Tweezers, medical scissors, and a reliable digital thermometer
Two to three pairs of sterile gloves (non-latex preferred)
A 7 to 14-day supply of all essential prescription medications for family members
An extra pair of prescription glasses or contact lenses, complete with solution and cases
Tools, Communication, and Light
When the grid goes down, the resulting darkness and isolation can be overwhelming and dangerous. Reliable light and communication tools are vital for maintaining safety, navigating your environment, and calling for rescue. It is critical that you never use candles or matches immediately after an earthquake due to the extreme risk of gas leaks and subsequent fires or explosions.
Multiple flashlights or headlamps (headlamps keep your hands free for moving debris) with a stockpile of extra batteries
A battery-powered or hand-crank NOAA Weather Radio to receive emergency broadcasts
A loud whistle to signal for help (three short blasts is the universal signal for distress)
A high-quality multi-tool or Swiss Army knife for minor repairs and opening stubborn items
A specialized wrench or sturdy pliers to quickly turn off gas and water utilities if you suspect a leak
Portable power banks, solar chargers, and necessary cables for your mobile phones
Physical, laminated local maps in case GPS services are entirely unavailable or cellular networks crash
Important Documents and Cash
In the chaotic aftermath of a disaster, proving your identity, accessing vital insurance policies, or simply paying for emergency supplies can become remarkably complicated. ATMs and credit card machines will not work without electricity, and networks may be down, so having physical cash in small denominations is crucial for survival.
Physical copies of personal identification, including driver's licenses, passports, and birth certificates
Copies of homeowners or renters insurance policies, property deeds, and vehicle titles
Recent bank account records, tax documents, and a list of important emergency contact numbers
Detailed medical information, including a comprehensive list of allergies, blood types, and current medications
Emergency cash in small bills ($1, $5, $10, $20) because vendors will likely not have change
Ensure you store all of these documents in a highly durable, waterproof, and portable container, or a small fireproof safe that can be easily carried. As a backup, you should also keep digital copies on an encrypted USB flash drive stored securely within your kit.
Special Considerations
A generic earthquake emergency kit checklist is an excellent starting point, but true, robust preparedness requires tailoring the kit to the unique individuals in your household. Take the necessary time to evaluate and plan for the specific, specialized needs of infants, seniors, people with disabilities, and your beloved pets.
For Babies and Toddlers: Liquid formula, extra diapers, bottles, powdered milk, diaper rash cream, wipes, and multiple changes of extra clothing tailored to the season
For Seniors and Disabled Individuals: Extra hearing aid batteries, wheelchair maintenance tools, specialized medical equipment, backup power supplies for necessary life-support devices, and clear written instructions for their care
For Pets: A minimum 72-hour supply of pet food and extra water, travel bowls, a sturdy leash, collar with updated ID tags, a travel carrier, veterinary records, and any pet medications
Where to Store Your Earthquake Kit
Because you never know exactly where you will be when a major quake strikes, it's highly recommended to prepare emergency supplies for multiple locations. Keep checking our
earthquakes near me
tool to stay aware of local seismic activity, but remember to be ready wherever you are—at home, at work, or on the road.
Home: Keep your primary, comprehensive kit in a designated place that is cool, dry, and easily accessible. A heavy-duty, waterproof plastic bin stored near a main exit or in a sturdy closet is ideal. Make sure all family members know exactly where it is.
Work: Be prepared to shelter in place at your workplace for at least 24 hours. A compact "go-bag" stored under your desk should contain comfortable walking shoes, water pouches, non-perishable snacks, a flashlight, and basic first aid items.
Car: In case you are stranded on the road during or after a quake, keep a smaller, self-contained kit in your trunk. Include jumper cables, a first aid kit, emergency flares, a warm blanket, water, protein bars, and a change of clothes.
How Often to Update Your Emergency Kit
An emergency kit is absolutely not a set-it-and-forget-it project. Over time, food supplies expire, batteries slowly corrode, medications lose their efficacy, and clothing sizes change (especially for rapidly growing children). Establish a strict, recurring rotation schedule to keep your supplies fresh, functional, and reliable. It's also important to remember that safety concerns persist even after the main shock has subsided; brush up on
aftershock safety
to ensure your kit and your knowledge support you through the entire event.
Set a repeating calendar reminder every six months—many safety organizations recommend tying this to Daylight Saving Time when you already change your smoke detector batteries. During this bi-annual check, meticulously replace expired food and water, test all electronics and replace batteries as needed, update your emergency contacts and medical records, and swap out stored clothing to match the upcoming season's weather.
